text: Mini-Lecture Notes Research skills step I Session 1 Part 2: Know your basics Learning objectives: 1. Differentiate between exposure and outcome in health research. 2. Explain what is meant by distribution of the disease 3. Calculate and interpret commonly used morbidity indicators. 4. Identify factors affecting disease frequency. Mini-Lecture Notes 2 Exposure and outcome Exposure and outcome are two terms that researchers use when they carry out clinical research. An exposure might also be called a risk factor or an independent variable, and it denotes the variable that the researcher is interested in seeing its effect of on a certain outcome, which is called the disease or the dependent variable. As an example, a researcher might be interested in studying the effect of physical activity (exposure) on obesity (outcome), but another researcher might be interested in studyin g the effect of obesity (exposure) on diabetes (outcome). Distribution of the disease: Description of the disease or health related phenomena in human population. It answers the following questions: 1. Who is getting the disease? (Person distribution) - chronic bronchitis is more encountered among men due to their smoking habit. - elderly are more exposed to fractures due to osteoporosis. 2. Where is the disease occurring? (Place distribution) - There is a marked difference between the incidences of each cancer in different parts of the world. - Accidents and mental illness are usually more frequent in urban than in rural areas however, bilharziasis is more frequent in rural areas than in urban areas. 3. When is it occurring? (Time distribution) - Upper respirato ry infections frequently show a seasonal rise in winter however, gastrointestinal infections are prominent in summer. - At one point of time, the occurrence in a community or region of cases of an illness, more than its normal expectancy is called “epidemic”. Mini-Lecture Notes 3 Measuring disease frequency: Why we need to measure diseases frequency? - Describe the extent and nature of the disease load in the community, and thus assist in establishment of priorities. - Needed for monitoring and evaluation of disease control activities. N: B. The word Morbidity refers to departure from a state of physical or psychological well-being, resulting from disease, illness, injury, or sickness. The most common rates used to measure morbidity (disease frequency) in a population are incidence and prevalence rates. I: Disease Prevalence Prevalence is the proportion of people in a population who have a particular disease at a specified point in time, or over a specified period. Prevalence is an indication of how frequent a specific outcome or disease is present in a specified population. It is most useful for measuring the burden of chronic diseases such as hypertension, diabetes mellitus and obesity in a population. Calculation of prevalence rate: The numerator is ALL individuals (old and new cases) who have a characteristic or a disease at a particular point in time (or during a particular period of time); the denominator is the population at risk of having the characteristic or the disease at this point in time or midway through a specific period. Mini-Lecture Notes 4 Incidence rate = The number of persons developing a disease (new cases in a specific period of time and locality) X 10n Total population at risk during the same period of time and locality For example, the prevalence of diabetes in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia during 2020 knowing that the number of diabetic patients equals 2000 patients and the total number of subjects included in the study equals 6,000 subjects. The prevalence of diabetes (Period prevalence during 2020)= (2000 /6000) X100=33.3% Factors affecting prevalence of the disease: 1. The rate of occurrence of new cases (disease incidence) 2. The duration of the disease (the effect of complete cure and death) 3. The quality of medical care for chronic diseases 4. Migration of cases or people at risk out of the country II: Disease Incidence: (Incidence rate IR) Incidence rate (IR): The rate at which new events occur in a population. The numerator is the number of NEW events that occur in a defined period; the denominator is the population at risk of experiencing this new event during the same period. N.B. Prevalence is distinct from incidence. Prevalence is a m easurement of all individuals (new and old) affected by the disease at a particular time, whereas incidence is a measurement of the number of new individuals who contract a disease during a particular period of time. Point Prevalence rate= The number of current cases (old+ new) of a specified disease existing at a given point of time x 10n The total population at the same point of time Period Prevalence rate= The number of current cases (old+ new) of a specified disease existing during a period of time x 10n The total population at the same period of time Mini-Lecture Notes 5 Example: Over the course of one year, 5 men are diagnosed with prostate cancer. Knowing that at the beginning of the study period , there were, 200 men that were free from prostatic cancer. calculate the incidence of prostatic cancer during this year? The number of new cases = 5 The population at risk= 200 The incidence rate = (5 / 200) X 100= 2.5% Factors affecting incidence of diseases 1. Increase in the proportion of population who has the risk factor (who are at risk). 2. Appearance of new risk factors for the disease in a community. 3. Change in the etiological factors e.g., mutation of organisms; influenza virus mutation and multi-drug resistance tuberculosis (MDR-TB). 4. Change in the effectiveness of the preventive program (either decrease or increase). 5. New diagnostic tools, screening p rograms, improved case finding, and reporting of diseases may lead to apparent (or false) increase in the incident cases. Relation between incidence and prevalence Figure 1: Relation between incidence and prevalence Figure 1 shows what is called prevalence pot . It demonstrates that new cases join pre -existing cases to make up total prevalence. However prevalent cases leave the prevalence pot in one of two ways: recovery or death.

text: Mini-Lecture Notes Research skills step I Lecture II The term “research” can be defined broadly as a process of solving problems and resolving previously unanswered questions. This is done by careful consideration or examination of a subject or occurrence. Although approach and specific objectives may vary, the ultimate goal of research always is to discover new knowledge. In biomedical research, this may include the description of a new phenomenon, the definition of a new relationship, the development of a new model, or the application of an existing principle or procedure to a new context. There are different research methods used in research, all with specific advantages an d disadvantages. Which one the scientist uses, depends on the aims of the study in addition to the nature of the phenomenon (topic), availability of data and resources (cost, time, human resources,). The main two types of research designs used in medicine are: 1. The quantitative research design , which generates numerical data or information that can be converted into numbers 2. The qualitative research design generates non-numerical data that provides a complete description of the research topic . e.g. conduction a focus group discussion or in -depth interview We will focus in our study on the quantitative research Mini-Lecture Notes 2 Study design: A study design is a scientific method that a researcher follows in his research. Mainly, it is the method based on which subjects included in the study are selected, observed, followed, and studied. We first can classify the study type into: 1. Primary research: It presents original data that appear for the first time. Data are not published before. 2. Secondary research: Data were published before, and the investigators retrive these data to summarize them, add them, reanalyze them, or synthesize new evidence from them. Secondary research includes collection, summary and/or synthesis of an evidence from existing research. What are the study designs for the primary clinical research? Primary research Observational research Iّ رInterventional research This type of studies does not involve any intervention or experiment. The researchers are observing some variables (characteristics) in a specific population without exposing the patients to a specific drug or intervention in the context of the research study. Example: When the investigator wants to estimate the magnitude (the prevalence) of anemia among under -five ch ildren in Alexandria and identify its risk factors(causes) This type of studies includes an intervention or an experimentation. This intervention might be a surgical operation, a drug, or any other form of treatment. The investigators manipulate this risk factor to examine its effect on this population. Example: when the investigator wants to test the effectiveness of measles vaccine in prevention of measles infection among under-five children in Alexandria Mini-Lecture Notes 3 Types of epidemiological studies I: Observational studies: Further classified into: 1. Descriptive studies: In which the main objective of the research is to describe certain characteristic (s) in the population. They are mainly characterized by absence of a well selected comparison (control) group. a. Ecological (population based) studies: They are studies in which the units of analysis are populations or groups of people rather than individuals b. Individual studies: • Case report • Case series report • Cross sectional design 2. Analytic studies: The main objective being beyond description as a specific association is assessed. it is mainly concerned with testing hypothesis regarding an association between certain exposure and an outcome. a. Case control study b. Cohort study 1. Descriptive studies: a. Ecological studies: In contrast to all other epidemiologic studies, the unit of analysis in ecological studies is populations, not individuals. they look for association between exposure and outcome in population using population averages. They rely on already available information or statistics. They compare data from different geographical regions or different population subgroups in the same region. Mini-Lecture Notes 4 Examples: The rate of dental caries in children was found to be much higher in areas with low levels of fluoridation in the water than in areas with high levels of natural fluoridation. (Association between frequency of dental caries and level of water flouridation in differen regions) Strengths: Easy, quick and inexpensive as data are available in records Suggest hypothesis about a possible relationship between two quantitative variables Limitations: Ecological studies provide no information about: Whether the people who were exposed to the characteristic were the same people who developed the disease. Whether the exposure or the onset of disease came first Whether there are other explanations for the observed association (confounding variables). • Figure : Relation between Cigarette Sales and Bladder Cancer for 44 States (Fraumeni, 1968) Mini-Lecture Notes 5 b. Individual studies: 1. Case report: Brief, objective report of a clinical characteristic or an outcome from a single subject or event, n = 1. It is usually a rare condition, unexplained condition, or a new symptom for a known disease. No control group. 2. Case series report: Objective report of a clinical characteristic or an outcome from a group of subjects , n >1. It usually includes a summary of the disease, such as the presentation (signs, symptoms), treatment course and treatment outcome. E.g., patients at a national hospital with treatment-resistant TB. A 61-year-old man with no significant medical history developed fever, headache and mild shortness of breath. He tested positive for SARS -CoV-2 and self -isolated at home, not requiring hospital admission. One week after testing positive, he developed acute severe burning pain affecting his whole body, subsequently localised distally in the limbs. There was no ataxia or autonomic failure. Neurological examination was unremarkable. Electrophysiological tests were unremarkable. Skin biopsy, lumbar puncture, enhanced MRI of the brachial plexus and MRI of the neuroaxis were normal. His pain was inadequately controlled with medication. This case highlights the variety of possible symptoms associated with SARS-CoV-2 infection. Conclusion: Cerebrovascular manifestations can occur in association with COVID -19 and may have significant implications on prognosis and management.
